title: CA SB1119: Companion chatbots: children’s safety.

obligations: Determine the age of a user pursuant to Title 1.81.9 (commencing with Section 1798.500) of Part 4 of Division 3 of the Civil Code, or if unable, rely on age determination made pursuant to subparagraph (B) of paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 27001 of the Health and Safety Code; alternatively apply child protections to all users except parental default settings cannot be changed unless actual knowledge user is not a child (Sec. 21811)

Before making a new or substantially modified companion chatbot available to users in the state, perform and document a comprehensive risk assessment related to design, configuration, and operation with respect to child users, containing summary of evaluation of each covered harm, methodology, benchmarks, consultations; take and document measures that reasonably mitigate any identified child safety risk (Sec. 21812(a))
If prohibiting child users, publish on internet website and update a high level description of how the operator complies with age assurance requirements (Sec. 21812(b))

If permitting child users, publish on internet website and update a child safety policy providing high level description of how chatbot is designed to prevent covered harms, how operator complies with age assurance, data restrictions, default settings, crisis response protocols, and measures implemented under Sec. 21812(d)(5)(A) (Sec. 21812(c))

Implement a documented crisis response protocol including timely in service support with referral to crisis service, actions for credible imminent threat, and clear age appropriate disclosures to child users linked to parent accounts (Sec. 21812(d)(1))
Implement safeguards for child users including usage reminders, clear age appropriate disclosures, and other protective design features (Sec. 21812(d)(2))

Implement default settings that can be changed only by a parent: disable persistent conversational memory, disable push notifications, limit single continuous usage session to one hour, limit total daily time to two hours; provide parental controls to adjust each default and disable access for child under 16; actively promote parental controls; if parent account not linked, default settings shall not be changed (Sec. 21812(d)(3))
Provide a mechanism for notice to child user that they are interacting with AI, reinforced periodically, in age appropriate language and format (Sec. 21812(d)(4))
Implement reasonable measures to prevent companion chatbot from doing listed harmful actions with respect to child user (Sec. 21812(d)(5))

Ensure interface design accessible and clear; test with representative samples of child users and parents on or before January 1, 2028 and every two years thereafter; document interface design decisions (Sec. 21812(d)(6))
Provide a public incident reporting mechanism enabling third party to report child safety risk incidents directly to operator (Sec. 21812(d)(7))

If operator has provided notice under Sec. 21812(d)(1)(B) or knows child user died or engaged in serious self harm based on conversations, notify parent if practicable and preserve records of conversation indicating serious self harm or risk for at least three years; not delete child user's account during preservation period (Sec. 21812.5)

Not display cross context behavioral advertising to child; not target advertising using personal information in conversational chat; label advertisements clearly and conspicuously; not sell personal information; not use or share personal information beyond necessary purposes; not use dark pattern with respect to interface designs related to features and controls under Section 21812 (Sec. 21813)

Ensure performance of child safety audit on or before January 1, 2029 or before first public availability, whichever later; every two years thereafter; before substantial modification with increased child safety risk; retain documentation for deployment plus five years; produce report with specified contents; retain unredacted copy; submit summary to Attorney General within 30 business days; post high level summary within 90 days (Sec. 21814)
prohibitions: Display to a child cross context behavioral advertising as defined in Section 1798.140 of the Civil Code (Sec. 21813(a)(1)(A))

Target advertising at a child user using personal information about the child in a conversational chat with the child, except age appropriate contextual advertising using specified categories (Sec. 21813(a)(1)(B))
Sell the personal information of a child user gathered through the companion chatbot (Sec. 21813(a)(2)(A))

Use or share the personal information of a child user gathered through the companion chatbot for any purpose beyond what is necessary to provide or maintain requested product or service, protect user safety security or service integrity, or comply with state or federal law or defend legal claims (Sec. 21813(a)(2)(B))
Use a dark pattern with respect to interface designs related to features and controls provided under Section 21812 (Sec. 21813(a)(2)(C))
If a parent account is not linked to the child user's account, the default settings shall not be changed (Sec. 21812(d)(3)(D))

An operator shall not delete a child user's account during the time period in which that account is associated with any record preserved pursuant to this section or the rules of state or federal civil procedure (Sec. 21812.5(b))

An operator shall not retain an independent third party auditor in which it has a financial interest or that has a financial interest in the operator, and shall not condition any payment or the amount of any payment on the results of the audit (Sec. 21814(b)(2)(C))

What it does

This law, known as Adam's Law, requires operators of companion chatbots to assess and mitigate child safety risks before making new or substantially modified chatbots available in California. It imposes age determination, child safety policies, default settings, parental controls, crisis protocols, data and advertising restrictions, and independent child safety audits. It authorizes enforcement by public prosecutors and private civil actions for actual harm to children.

Who it applies to

  • Operators of companion chatbots available to users in California, except postsecondary educational institutions making chatbots exclusively for educational settings and entities making chatbots exclusively for employees, contractors, or other personnel in workplace settings (Sec. 21810.5(j))
  • Operators who allow child users once age has been determined pursuant to Section 21811, except for Section 21811, subdivision (b) of Section 21812, and Section 21816 which apply to all operators (Sec. 21810.5(j)(1)(B))

Effective date

The text does not state a general effective date. Operative dates are July 1, 2027 for Sections 21812, 21812.5, and 21813 (Sec. 21812(e), Sec. 21812.5(d), Sec. 21813(b)). Section 21814 has two versions with conditional operative dates depending on whether Assembly Bill 1405 is chaptered and takes effect on or before January 1, 2027 (Sec. 21814(g) and Sec. 21814(f)).

Key definitions

  • Child: a natural person under 18 years of age (Sec. 21810.5(a))
  • Child safety audit: an audit conducted by an independent third party auditor to assess internal controls, processes, and systems implemented for a companion chatbot that are necessary for compliance with this chapter (Sec. 21810.5(b))
  • Child safety policy: a public facing document describing protective measures taken by an operator to mitigate identified child safety risks (Sec. 21810.5(c))
  • Child safety risk: a reasonably foreseeable risk of a covered harm to a child (Sec. 21810.5(d))
  • Child sexual abuse material: has the meaning defined in Section 3273.65 of the Civil Code (Sec. 21810.5(e))
  • Companion chatbot: has the meaning defined in Section 22601 (Sec. 21810.5(f))
  • Covered harm: any of the following harms caused by the child's use of a companion chatbot: reasonably foreseeable physical or financial harm; severe and reasonably foreseeable psychological or emotional harm to a reasonable child; a highly offensive intrusion on privacy rights protected by state or federal law; adverse discrimination in violation of state or federal law (Sec. 21810.5(g))
  • Dark pattern: a design choice that has the substantial effect of subverting or impairing user autonomy, decisionmaking, or choice (Sec. 21810.5(h))
  • Obscene matter: has the meaning defined in Section 311 of the Penal Code (Sec. 21810.5(i))
  • Operator: a person who makes a companion chatbot available to a user in the state; except for Section 21811, subdivision (b) of Section 21812, and Section 21816, operator applies only to an operator who allows child users once age has been determined pursuant to Section 21811; does not include a postsecondary educational institution that makes a companion chatbot available exclusively for use in educational settings, or an entity when making a companion chatbot available exclusively to employees, contractors, or other personnel for use in workplace settings (Sec. 21810.5(j))
  • Parent: a parent or legal guardian; does not include a parent of an emancipated youth with respect to the use of a companion chatbot by that emancipated youth (Sec. 21810.5(k))
  • Parental control: a feature that enables a parent to support a child's use of a companion chatbot, including through usage limits, feature restrictions, or transparency tools (Sec. 21810.5(l))
  • Persistent conversational memory: a companion chatbot's incorporation of prior conversations for use in future conversations; does not include the use of information necessary to ensure the child's safety, identify a user, enable user preferences, including, but not limited to, educational settings, or maintain device configuration (Sec. 21810.5(m))
  • Personal information: has the meaning defined in Section 1798.140 of the Civil Code (Sec. 21810.5(n))
  • Substantial modification: a new version, new release, or other update to a companion chatbot that materially changes its functionality or performance (Sec. 21810.5(o))
  • Trade secret: has the meaning defined in Section 3426.1 of the Civil Code (Sec. 21810.5(p))

Obligations

  • Determine the age of a user pursuant to Title 1.81.9 (commencing with Section 1798.500) of Part 4 of Division 3 of the Civil Code, or if unable, rely on age determination made pursuant to subparagraph (B) of paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 27001 of the Health and Safety Code; alternatively apply child protections to all users except parental default settings cannot be changed unless actual knowledge user is not a child (Sec. 21811)
  • Before making a new or substantially modified companion chatbot available to users in the state, perform and document a comprehensive risk assessment related to design, configuration, and operation with respect to child users, containing summary of evaluation of each covered harm, methodology, benchmarks, consultations; take and document measures that reasonably mitigate any identified child safety risk (Sec. 21812(a))
  • If prohibiting child users, publish on internet website and update a high level description of how the operator complies with age assurance requirements (Sec. 21812(b))
  • If permitting child users, publish on internet website and update a child safety policy providing high level description of how chatbot is designed to prevent covered harms, how operator complies with age assurance, data restrictions, default settings, crisis response protocols, and measures implemented under Sec. 21812(d)(5)(A) (Sec. 21812(c))
  • Implement a documented crisis response protocol including timely in service support with referral to crisis service, actions for credible imminent threat, and clear age appropriate disclosures to child users linked to parent accounts (Sec. 21812(d)(1))
  • Implement safeguards for child users including usage reminders, clear age appropriate disclosures, and other protective design features (Sec. 21812(d)(2))
  • Implement default settings that can be changed only by a parent: disable persistent conversational memory, disable push notifications, limit single continuous usage session to one hour, limit total daily time to two hours; provide parental controls to adjust each default and disable access for child under 16; actively promote parental controls; if parent account not linked, default settings shall not be changed (Sec. 21812(d)(3))
  • Provide a mechanism for notice to child user that they are interacting with AI, reinforced periodically, in age appropriate language and format (Sec. 21812(d)(4))
  • Implement reasonable measures to prevent companion chatbot from doing listed harmful actions with respect to child user (Sec. 21812(d)(5))
  • Ensure interface design accessible and clear; test with representative samples of child users and parents on or before January 1, 2028 and every two years thereafter; document interface design decisions (Sec. 21812(d)(6))
  • Provide a public incident reporting mechanism enabling third party to report child safety risk incidents directly to operator (Sec. 21812(d)(7))
  • If operator has provided notice under Sec. 21812(d)(1)(B) or knows child user died or engaged in serious self harm based on conversations, notify parent if practicable and preserve records of conversation indicating serious self harm or risk for at least three years; not delete child user's account during preservation period (Sec. 21812.5)
  • Not display cross context behavioral advertising to child; not target advertising using personal information in conversational chat; label advertisements clearly and conspicuously; not sell personal information; not use or share personal information beyond necessary purposes; not use dark pattern with respect to interface designs related to features and controls under Section 21812 (Sec. 21813)
  • Ensure performance of child safety audit on or before January 1, 2029 or before first public availability, whichever later; every two years thereafter; before substantial modification with increased child safety risk; retain documentation for deployment plus five years; produce report with specified contents; retain unredacted copy; submit summary to Attorney General within 30 business days; post high level summary within 90 days (Sec. 21814)

Prohibitions

  • Display to a child cross context behavioral advertising as defined in Section 1798.140 of the Civil Code (Sec. 21813(a)(1)(A))
  • Target advertising at a child user using personal information about the child in a conversational chat with the child, except age appropriate contextual advertising using specified categories (Sec. 21813(a)(1)(B))
  • Sell the personal information of a child user gathered through the companion chatbot (Sec. 21813(a)(2)(A))
  • Use or share the personal information of a child user gathered through the companion chatbot for any purpose beyond what is necessary to provide or maintain requested product or service, protect user safety security or service integrity, or comply with state or federal law or defend legal claims (Sec. 21813(a)(2)(B))
  • Use a dark pattern with respect to interface designs related to features and controls provided under Section 21812 (Sec. 21813(a)(2)(C))
  • If a parent account is not linked to the child user's account, the default settings shall not be changed (Sec. 21812(d)(3)(D))
  • An operator shall not delete a child user's account during the time period in which that account is associated with any record preserved pursuant to this section or the rules of state or federal civil procedure (Sec. 21812.5(b))
  • An operator shall not retain an independent third party auditor in which it has a financial interest or that has a financial interest in the operator, and shall not condition any payment or the amount of any payment on the results of the audit (Sec. 21814(b)(2)(C))

Penalties and enforcement

Public prosecutors described in Section 17204 may bring civil action for violations of this chapter to obtain civil penalty up to $5,000 per affected child for each negligent violation, up to $15,000 per affected child for each intentional violation, injunctive or declaratory relief for Attorney General only, reasonable attorney's fees, and other relief; penalties collected paid to prosecutor office, Attorney General penalties to Public Rights Law Enforcement Special Fund (Sec. 21816(a)). A child who suffers actual harm as a result of violation of paragraphs (1) to (5) of subdivision (d) of Section 21812, or parent or guardian on behalf, may bring civil action for actual damages, attorney's fees and costs, injunctive or declaratory relief, other relief; financial harm must exceed $1,000 per child; emotional harm must constitute serious emotional distress (Sec. 21816(b)). A violation of this chapter shall not constitute a basis for private cause of action under Unfair Competition Law (Sec. 21816(c)). The Attorney General may for cause request and obtain a copy of AI child safety audit report; report submitted to AG is confidential but may be used for enforcement (Sec. 21814(d),(e)). Lead auditor certifies results under penalty of perjury (Sec. 21814(a)(4)(I)). Attorney General shall establish public incident reporting mechanism by January 1, 2028 (Sec. 21815).

How it affects AI deployment

  • Before deploying a new or substantially modified companion chatbot in California, an organisation must perform and document a comprehensive child safety risk assessment and implement mitigations (Sec. 21812(a)).
  • The organisation must determine user age or apply child protections to all users, which affects onboarding and account setup (Sec. 21811).
  • If child users are permitted, the organisation must publish a child safety policy and implement numerous technical safeguards including default settings, parental controls, crisis response protocols, AI notices, and measures to prevent specified harmful chatbot behaviors (Sec. 21812(c),(d)).
  • The organisation must restrict advertising and data practices for child users, including no cross context behavioral advertising, no sale of personal information, and limited use and sharing (Sec. 21813).
  • The organisation must undergo independent child safety audits every two years and before substantial modifications with increased risk, retain documentation, submit summaries to the Attorney General, and post high level summaries (Sec. 21814).
  • The organisation must preserve conversation records and notify parents in cases of serious self harm or death, and cannot delete associated accounts during preservation (Sec. 21812.5).
  • Noncompliance can lead to civil penalties up to $15,000 per affected child per intentional violation and private lawsuits for actual harm (Sec. 21816).

Notable exemptions

  • Postsecondary educational institutions making companion chatbots exclusively for educational settings are not operators (Sec. 21810.5(j)(2)(A)).
  • Entities making companion chatbots available exclusively to employees, contractors, or other personnel for workplace settings are not operators (Sec. 21810.5(j)(2)(B)).
  • Parent does not include parent of emancipated youth with respect to use by that emancipated youth (Sec. 21810.5(k)(2)).
  • Persistent conversational memory does not include use of information necessary to ensure child safety, identify user, enable user preferences including educational settings, or maintain device configuration (Sec. 21810.5(m)(2)).
  • For child users 16 or older, storing past conversations that a child can elect to continue is not persistent conversational memory if not used to construct durable profiles (Sec. 21812(d)(3)(A)(i)(II)(ia)).
  • Product or service recommendations that a user explicitly requests in conversation are not considered facilitating advertising (Sec. 21812(d)(5)(B)(ix)(II)).
  • Paragraph (5) does not prohibit a companion chatbot from providing age appropriate information or resources concerning abuse, neglect, bullying, or other unsafe circumstances (Sec. 21812(d)(5)(B)).
  • Before January 1, 2032, operators with less than $500 million gross revenue in prior calendar year are not required to comply with audit section (Sec. 21814(f) or Sec. 21814(c) depending on version).
  • A single risk assessment may be completed for a comparable set of companion chatbots, and a risk assessment conducted for another law may be used if substantially similar scope and effect (Sec. 21812(a)(2),(3)).
  • A single child safety audit may be performed for comparable chatbots, and an independent audit for another law may be used if substantially similar scope (Sec. 21814(a)(1)(B),(2)).
  • Operator may impose security protocols on auditor to protect trade secrets, confidential business information, cybersecurity, individual privacy, or public safety (Sec. 21814(a)(3)(B)).
  • Operator may make reasonable redactions to protect trade secrets and individual privacy when providing audit report to Attorney General (Sec. 21814(d)(2)(A)).
  • This chapter shall not be construed to require an operator to take an action that violates federal law (Sec. 21818).

Compliance steps

  • Determine whether the organisation is an operator under Sec. 21810.5(j), including whether any exemption applies.
  • Establish age determination process or apply child protections to all users (Sec. 21811).
  • Before making a new or substantially modified companion chatbot available, perform and document comprehensive risk assessment and implement mitigations (Sec. 21812(a)).
  • Publish required website disclosures: age assurance compliance description if prohibiting child users, or child safety policy if permitting child users (Sec. 21812(b),(c)).
  • Implement all child protection requirements under Sec. 21812(d): crisis response protocol, safeguards, default settings, parental controls, AI notice, measures to prevent harmful behaviors, interface design and testing, public incident reporting.
  • Comply with data and advertising restrictions under Sec. 21813.
  • Establish procedures for parent notification and record preservation under Sec. 21812.5.
  • Ensure independent child safety audit is performed on schedule, retain documentation, submit summary to Attorney General within 30 business days, and post high level summary within 90 days (Sec. 21814).
  • Monitor for incidents and respond to Attorney General requests for audit reports (Sec. 21814(d), Sec. 21815).

LEGISLATIVE COUNSEL'S DIGEST SB 1119, Padilla.
 Companion chatbots: children’s safety. Existing law generally regulates artificial intelligence, including companion chatbots, as defined. Existing law requires an operator, as defined, to prevent a companion chatbot on its companion chatbot platform from engaging with users unless the operator maintains a protocol for preventing the production of suicidal ideation, suicide, or self-harm content to the user. Existing law requires an operator, for a user the operator knows is a minor, to take certain prescribed action, including disclosing to the user that the user is interacting with artificial intelligence. This bill would delete those provisions imposing requirements on an operator if the operator knows the user is a minor. The Digital Age Assurance Act requires a person who owns, maintains, or controls a software application, as
 defined, to request age bracket data sent by a real-time secure application programming interface or operating system with respect to a particular user from an operating system provider or a covered application store when the application is downloaded and launched. This bill would require an operator, as defined, of a companion chatbot to, beginning July 1, 2027, before making a new or substantially modified companion chatbot available to
 users in the state, do various things with respect to child safety, including perform and document a comprehensive risk assessment related to the design, configuration, and operation of the companion chatbot with respect to minor users that contains, among other things, a summary of the results of any evaluation of each covered harm, as defined, pertaining to the companion chatbot. The bill would require an operator to submit to independent child safety audits of its compliance with the bill, as
 specified. The bill would require an auditor to produce a report that describes whether the operator has established and adhered to policies and practices to comply with the bill that includes, among other things, the signature of the lead auditor certifying the results of the audit under penalty of perjury. By expanding the scope of the crime of perjury, this bill would impose a state-mandated local program. The bill would authorize the Attorney General to, for cause, request and obtain a copy of an AI child safety audit report from the operator and would make a child safety audit report submitted to the Attorney General confidential. This bill would authorize certain public prosecutors to bring a civil action to enforce the bill’s provisions, as specified, and would authorize a child who suffers an actual harm as a result of a violation of this chapter, or a parent or guardian acting on behalf of that
 child, to bring a civil action against the operator, as specified. Existing constitutional provisions require that a statute that limits the right of access to the meetings of public bodies or the writings of public officials and agencies be adopted with findings demonstrating the interest protected by the limitation and the need for protecting that interest. This bill would make legislative findings to that effect. The California Constitution requires the state to reimburse local agencies and school districts for certain costs mandated by the state. Statutory provisions establish procedures
 for making that reimbursement. This bill would provide that no reimbursement is required by this act for a specified reason. Digest Key

 Article I of the California Constitution.
